FULL VIEW
OUTLINE VIEW
Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Describe the role of the glenohumeral joint anatomy in providing shoulder stability.
Obtain the history of and perform a physical examination in patients with traumatic and
atraumatic shoulder instability.
Recognize traumatic shoulder instability on imaging studies.
Apply common treatment options for shoulder instability.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Laxity is a physiologic term that refers to the passive translation of the humeral head on the
glenoid or over the glenoid rim. Laxity may be pathologic or physiologic.
Glenohumeral instability is a pathologic state in which glenohumeral laxity causes pain,
subluxation, or dislocation.




Classification
Glenohumeral instability represents a spectrum of pathology based on the direction of the
laxity (anterior, posterior, or multidirectional) and the underlying cause (traumatic or
atraumatic).
A spectrum of instability exists, and patients may initially experience a traumatic event
followed by atraumatic instability events.
In patients with traumatic and atraumatic events, recognition of underlying ligamentous laxity
or collagen disorders is important.

Classification
Laxity of the shoulder joint is multifactorial and may involve subluxation and/or
dislocation. Instability can occur in multiple directions because of the mobility of the
shoulder joint. An underlying connective tissue disorder and/or trauma may be
responsible. In addition, many patients may have atraumatic and traumatic instability.
Understanding the etiology of shoulder instability is especially critical in the highly active
pediatric and adolescent population.
Anatomy
Glenohumeral stability depends on active and passive restraints.
Passive restraints: The primary passive restraint is the labrum, a cartilaginous ring that
encircles the bony glenoid, deepening the glenoid fossa and serving as an attachment site for
capsuloligamentous structures. The glenohumeral ligaments form a second important
passive restraint and attach to the glenoid and labrum (Figure 1).
The anterior band of the inferior glenohumeral ligament (IGHL) is the primary restraint to
anterior translation of the humeral head with the arm in abduction and external rotation.
The posterior band of the IGHL is the primary restraint to posterior translation of the
humeral head with the arm in forward flexion and adduction.
The superior glenohumeral ligament, middle glenohumeral ligament, and coracohumeral
ligament also play important roles in glenohumeral stability.

Active restraints: The rotator cuff muscles and the deltoid are the main active restraints to
glenohumeral instability.
Figure 1 Photograph shows the anatomy of the glenohumeral capsule and its thickenings, called
glenohumeral ligaments. Table shows the primary function of each anatomic structure. AIGHL =
anterior band of the inferior glenohumeral ligament, BT = biceps tendon, MGHL = middle
glenohumeral ligament, PIGHL = posterior band of the inferior glenohumeral ligament, SGHL =
superior glenohumeral ligament. (Image reproduced with permission from Itoigawa Y, Itoi E:
Anatomy of capsulolabral complex and rotator interval related to glenohumeral instability. Knee
Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc 24[2]:343-349. Table reproduced from Riboh JC, Singh A: Shoulder
instability, rotator cuff disorders, muscular ruptures, adhesive capsulitis, calcific tendinitis, in
Parvizi J, ed: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update, ed 13. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of
Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2021, pp 281-300.)

Anatomy
The shoulder joint contains passive and active restraints to shoulder instability. The
passive restraints, which include the capsule/labrum and glenohumeral ligaments,
typically are repaired by surgical management. Active restraints, which are not typically
injured during a traumatic instability event in the pediatric/adolescent population,
usually are strengthened via physical therapy.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:30 AM
AAOS | Shoulder Instability
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000034
3/28

Etiology
Shoulder instability in the pediatric and adolescent population typically involves a traumatic
episode in which the humeral head dislocates from the glenoid anteroinferiorly. Subluxation
events also can occur.
Traumatic anterior instability: anterior glenohumeral dislocation resulting from a traumatic
event with an anteriorly directed force and the arm positioned in abduction and external
rotation
Traumatic posterior instability: posterior glenohumeral dislocation resulting from a traumatic
event with a posteriorly directed force on the arm positioned in forward flexion and
adduction
Acquired/atraumatic instability: pathologic glenohumeral laxity resulting from repetitive
trauma to the capsule and the intraarticular structures of the shoulder (eg, as in overhead
throwing athletes)
Multidirectional instability: pathologic glenohumeral laxity with recurrent subluxation or
dislocation in more than one direction

Etiology
In this age group, most instability events involve traumatic anterior instability in which
the arm is forcefully placed in an abducted and externally rotated position. Posterior
instability typically is observed during seizures or in athletes with a shoulder that is
repetitively forced posteriorly (eg, football lineman). Atraumatic instability may occur in
overhead throwing athletes as a result of internal rotation deficits from repetitive
throwing. Multidirectional instability also may occur in this population and often is
accompanied by the ability to voluntarily dislocate or subluxate.
Natural History
Pediatric and adolescent patients have a high incidence of repeated instability episodes (as
high as 100%) if treated nonsurgically, particularly young males involved in collision sports.1-3
Athletes who experience traumatic instability events typically can return to activity within 1 to
3 weeks; however, a high rate of repeated instability occurs during the season.4,5
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:30 AM
AAOS | Shoulder Instability
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000034
4/28

Patients who have recurrent shoulder instability events have an increased risk of
glenohumeral arthritis.6

Natural History
If treated nonsurgically, patients younger than 18 years have a very high likelihood of
sustaining repeated instability events because many of these individuals participate in
collision sports. Repetitive instability events not only preclude sporting activity but also
may increase the risk of glenohumeral arthritis. Therefore, in this age group surgical
stabilization of shoulders is becoming more common earlier in the disease course rather
than later.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Traumatic Anterior Instability
Epidemiology
Incidence: Traumatic anterior shoulder dislocation is the most common form of glenohumeral
instability in this age group, representing 88% to 98% of all dislocations.
Recurrence rate: Although age at the time of initial dislocation is considered the primary risk
factor for re-dislocation, new studies have suggested a more complex scenario, also
implicating sex, activity level, and bony lesions to the humeral head and glenoid as risk factors
Pathoanatomy
Anterior glenohumeral dislocation typically occurs secondary to a traumatic event involving
excessive abduction and external rotation that causes anterior and inferior displacement of
the humeral head over the glenoid.
A Bankart lesion (detachment of the anteroinferior labrum and the anterior band of the IGHL
complex) is an important pathoanatomic finding in 90% of patients with a traumatic
glenohumeral dislocation (Figure 2).
Patients who experience higher energy injuries with or without recurrent dislocations also may
have a bony component to their injury and a glenoid fracture (ie, bony Bankart) (Figure 3).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:30 AM
AAOS | Shoulder Instability
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000034
5/28

A Hill-Sachs lesion is a compression fracture of the posterosuperior humeral head caused by
its impaction on the anteroinferior glenoid rim after dislocation (Figure 4).
Hill-Sachs lesions occur in as many as 80% of patients with an anterior dislocation.
Understanding the concept of the glenoid track in relation to a Hill-Sachs defect is important
(Figure 5).
The contact zone of the glenoid with the humeral head is the glenoid track.7
On-track lesion: a Hill-Sachs lesion that cannot engage the glenoid; therefore, the instability
risk decreases
Off-track lesion: a Hill Sachs lesion that can engage the glenoid; therefore, the instability risk
increases
After instability events, the risk of off-track lesions is higher in adolescent patients than adult
patients.8
Other injuries that may be observed include a torn labrum healing to the medial aspect of the
glenoid neck (ie, anterior labroligamentous periosteal sleeve avulsion), humeral avulsion of the
glenohumeral ligaments [HAGL] lesion, and rotator cuff injury).
Concomitant injury to the brachial plexus occurs in 13.5% of patients. An axillary nerve injury is
most common, followed by a mixed plexus injury.

Figure 5 Three-dimensional CT scans show the technique for measuring the glenoid track. The
length of the glenoid track is 83% of the maximum anterior-to-posterior diameter of the glenoid
(A). The glenoid track length is then projected onto the humeral head extending medial from the
rotator cuff attachment (R), creating the glenoid track line (G) on the humerus. This is then
compared with the position of the Hill-Sachs defect (red dotted line, B). A defect that extends
medial to G is considered off-track. If glenoid bone loss is present, the width of the defect (d)
must be subtracted from the glenoid track. Therefore, the original glenoid track line on the
humerus (G2) must be brought laterally by the same distance (d) to create a more accurate line
(G1), accounting for the bipolar bone loss. (Reproduced with permission from Di Giacomo G, Itoi
E, Burkhart SS: Evolving concept of bipolar bone loss and the Hill-Sachs lesion: From
“engaging/non-engaging” lesion to “on-track/off-track” lesion. Arthroscopy 2014;30[1]:90-98.)

Traumatic Anterior Instability
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:30 AM
AAOS | Shoulder Instability
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000034
10/28

Because traumatic anterior shoulder instability is the most common shoulder pathology
in this age group, an understanding of this injury is crucial. Although age is a major risk
factor for recurrence, the risk of re-dislocation is multifactorial and may be attributed to
factors such as activity level and degree of bony involvement.
During a traumatic anterior dislocation, a Bankart lesion typically occurs because of
damage to the anteroinferior labrum and the anterior IGHL. This may be accompanied
by a fracture of the glenoid (ie, bony Bankart), which increases the risk of recurrence and
may preclude arthroscopic approaches to management. In addition, injury to the
posterosuperior humeral head (Hill-Sachs lesion) should be identified and evaluated. The
risk of instability may increase if the lesion engages the glenoid (ie, off-track). The risk of
these lesions is higher in the pediatric and adolescent population than in the adult
population.
Finally, other pathology observed on MRI should be identified and evaluated, particularly
HAGL lesions, which may be missed during routine arthroscopy. In addition, nerve
injuries resulting from traumatic instability should be documented and monitored.
Evaluation
Patient History
Traumatic anterior shoulder instability typically occurs during high-energy activity.
Reports of acute onset of shoulder pain, weakness, and occasionally paresthesias in the
axillary nerve distribution
Physical Examination
Neurovascular examination with documentation of axillary motor and sensory function
Shoulder range of motion and strength (compared with noninjured side)
Apprehension and relocation test: The arm is abducted and externally rotated to 90°. A feeling
of apprehension at 90° is suggestive of injury. Apprehension at 45° suggests glenoid bone loss
and labral injury.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:30 AM
AAOS | Shoulder Instability
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000034
11/28

Load and shift test: The humeral head is translated anteriorly while the scapula/glenoid is
stabilized. The degree of translation is grade I, increased translation without subluxation;
grade II, subluxation in which the humeral head translates to the glenoid rim but not over it; or
grade III, dislocation over the glenoid rim.
Sulcus sign: The affected arm is pulled inferiorly. If a sulcus forms between the humerus and
acromion, multidirectional instability is indicated.
The patient also should be assessed for generalized hypermobility via the Beighton
hypermobility score.9

Evaluation
The initial examination of the patient, on the field or in the emergency department, may
be difficult. Therefore, many of the aforementioned maneuvers may need to be
performed 7 to 10 days post injury, at which time early soft-tissue healing has occurred.
In every patient, a careful neurovascular examination should be performed. The goals of
the physical examination are to confirm the diagnosis, assess the degree and/or
direction of instability, and understand global shoulder function.
Diagnostic Studies
Radiographs: True shoulder AP (Grashey view), scapular AP, and axillary views (or Velpeau view
if standard axillary view cannot be tolerated) are standard radiographic views (Figure 6).
Other helpful views include the West Point view (to visualize glenoid bone loss) and the Stryker
notch view (to visualize Hill-Sachs lesions).
Ruling out a Salter Harris type I or type II proximal humerus injury or other fractures that may
mimic shoulder dislocation is essential.
The need for advanced imaging studies for first-time shoulder dislocations in the pediatric and
adolescent population is controversial.
Recurrent instability in the adolescent population is associated with bony pathology and
increasing bone loss with subsequent dislocations.
Understanding the degree of soft-tissue injury, the degree of glenoid bone loss, and the size
and/or location of a Hill-Sachs lesion are critical for treatment planning.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:30 AM
AAOS | Shoulder Instability
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000034
12/28

MRI is useful for evaluating soft-tissue details, labral lesions, bony injury to the glenoid, the
presence and type of Hill-Sachs lesion (eg, on-track versus off-track), rotator cuff pathology,
and HAGL or anterior labroligamentous periosteal sleeve avulsion lesions (Figure 7). With the
advent of 3T MRI, magnetic resonance arthrography is not necessarily indicated to assess the
degree of intraarticular pathology in patients with shoulder instability. If standard MRI is
inconclusive, then magnetic resonance arthrography may be performed.
CT is useful for additional detailed evaluation of bony injuries.
Figure 6 AP radiograph of the right shoulder shows an anterior dislocation of the humeral head
(arrow). Note that the humeral head is inferior and medial to the glenoid fossa. (Reproduced
Blaine T: Glenohumeral instability, in Johnson TR, Steinbach LS, eds: Essentials of Musculoskeletal
Imaging. Rosemont, IL, Americna Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2004, pp 196-201.)
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:30 AM
AAOS | Shoulder Instability
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000034
13/28

Figure 7 MRIs show glenohumeral pathology in two separate shoulders. A, Coronal T2-weighted
MRI shows a humeral avulsion of the glenohumeral ligament. B, Abduction and external rotation
MRI shows an anteroinferior labral tear in a patient experiencing recurrent subluxations who did
not have pathology observed on other imaging sequences. This correlated with arthroscopic
findings at time of repair. (Reproduced from Patzkowski JC, Owens BD: Shoulder instability, in
Miller MD, ed. Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Sports Medicine, ed 5. Rosemont, IL, American
Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2016, pp 3-16.)

Diagnostic Studies
If a shoulder instability event is suspected, radiographs should be obtained to document
reduction and rule out other pathology, such as proximal humerus fractures, clavicle
fractures, and acromioclavicular joint injuries. The use of advanced imaging studies (ie,
MRI) for first-time shoulder dislocations has increased because of the risk of recurrent
instability in this patient population. MRI allows for assessment of Bankart lesions,
glenoid bone loss, the presence and type of Hill-Sachs lesions, and other concomitant
pathology in the shoulder joint that may require or complicate management. If
additional quantification of glenoid or humeral head bone loss is required, then CT may
be performed.
Management
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:30 AM
AAOS | Shoulder Instability
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000034
14/28

In the adolescent population, optimal management of first-time shoulder dislocations is
controversial.10-12
Critical bone loss is a risk with repeated instability events.8,13
Nonsurgical Management
Nonsurgical treatment is appropriate for patients with multidirectional instability, low activity
demands, and medical contraindications.
Acute dislocations
Rest, ice, and anti-inflammatories
Position and duration of immobilization are controversial14
Physical therapy that focuses on painless symmetric range of motion followed by
strengthening (without apprehension) allows for a return to sports activity.
Evidence on the efficacy of bracing to prevent re-dislocation is conflicting.4,5
High rate of recurrence, which may necessitate surgical management in the off-season4,5
Multidirectional instability
Emphasis on physical therapy and activity modifications
Surgical management as a last resort because of high risk of recurrence

Nonsurgical Management
The trend toward surgical fixation in patients with unilateral traumatic anterior instability
is increasing. The combination of participation in higher risk sports activity with a greater
degree of internal (particularly bony) injuries during instability events has sparked this
evolution. Regardless, nonsurgical management remains the first-line treatment option
for patients with low activity demands, patients with medical comorbidities, and patients
who prefer in-season sports participation. For these patients, a brief period of
immobilization should be followed by a graduated physical therapy program focused on
shoulder range of motion before strength and functional testing is performed. Patients
with multidirectional instability should undergo surgical stabilization only as a last resort,
with physical therapy being the mainstay of management.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:30 AM
AAOS | Shoulder Instability
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000034

Surgical Management
Surgical Indications
Failure of nonsurgical management with recurrent instability
Patients younger than 18 years who engage in athletics or other high-demand activities may
benefit from immediate surgical stabilization.
Patients with major bony injuries also may require surgical stabilization.
Increased activity demands, high rate of recurrent instability, soft-tissue quality, and bony
involvement help determine management.15, 16, 17
Preoperative Planning
All imaging studies reviewed
Careful understanding of MRI/CT to determine the quality of the labrum and any additional
pathology (ie, rotator cuff, superior labrum anterior to posterior, posterior labrum, HAGL), Hill-
Sachs lesions (off-track versus on-track), and the degree of glenoid bone loss (Figure 8)
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:30 AM
AAOS | Shoulder Instability
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000034
16/28

Figure 8 Three-dimensional CT scans show two general techniques for calculating the percentage
of glenoid bone loss. The benchmark is to obtain bilateral three-dimensional CT scans. A perfect
circle that best fits the inferior two-thirds of the uninjured glenoid is created, and its surface area
is measured (A). This circle is then projected onto the injured glenoid. The surface area of injured
glenoid contained within this circle (B) is then measured, and the percentage of glenoid bone loss
is calculated as (A – B)/(A) × 100%. If a CT scan of only the injured shoulder is available, then a
perfect circle estimating the inferior two-thirds of the native glenoid is created, with radius B. The
distance from the center of this circle to the true glenoid edge anteriorly (A) is then measured.
The percentage of bone loss is calculated as (B – A)/(2 × B) ×100% (bottom panel). (Reproduced
with permission from Bakshi NK, Cibulas GA, Sekiya JK, Bedi A: A clinical comparison of linear- and
surface area–based methods of measuring glenoid bone loss. Am J Sports Med 2018;46[10]:2472-
2477.)
Surgical Technique
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:30 AM
AAOS | Shoulder Instability
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000034
17/28

Anterior labrum pathology, less than 25% glenoid bone loss, and an on-track Hill-Sachs lesion:
arthroscopic labral repair
Anterior labrum pathology, less than 25% glenoid bone loss, and an off-track Hill-Sachs lesion:
arthroscopic labral repair and remplissage 18-21
Anterior labrum pathology and more than 25% glenoid bone loss: open Latarjet procedure
(rarely performed in the skeletally immature population)
Historically, open Bankart repair has been used to treat patients; however, arthroscopic
shoulder techniques are associated with less pain and greater preservation of motion.22
Patient Positioning
Beach-chair versus lateral decubitus position with traction device (arthroscopic) (Figure 9)
Beach-chair position (open procedures)
Before positioning and while the patient is under anesthesia, the direction and degree of
instability should be documented.
Figure 9 Intraoperative photograph shows the lateral decubitus position with the use of a
traction device. (Reproduced from Yi SJ, Koh JL: The beach-chair and lateral decubitus positions:
Key surgical principles, in Abrams JS, Bell RH, Tokish JM, eds: Advanced Reconstruction: Shoulder, ed
2. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2016, pp 3-8.)
Technique/Procedures/Equipment
Suture anchors (knotless, all-suture, biocomposite, polyether ether ketone, metallic),
arthroscopic cannulas, 4-mm 30° and 70° arthroscopes, nonabsorbable suture, rasp/liberator,
graspers, knot pusher, and suture passers
Standard diagnostic arthroscopy should address all pathology.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:30 AM
AAOS | Shoulder Instability
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000034
18/28

The typical arthroscopic procedure for traumatic anterior instability is arthroscopic labral
reconstruction with capsular shift.
Remplissage is added for off-track Hill-Sachs lesions.
If a bony piece is less than 25% of the glenoid, it can be reduced to the glenoid and
incorporated into the repair during labral fixation.
Arthroscopic labral repair (Figure 10)
Preparation of the labrum is key, with use of a rasp to liberate and mobilize the labrum
followed by a burr/shaver to prepare the glenoid for anchors.
A suture lasso or other suture passing device is used to grasp the labrum and capsule.
Mobilization of the capsule anterosuperiorly with the labrum is critical.
Knotless or traditional suture anchors can be used for fixation.
Use of fewer than three anchors has been associated with failure.23
Placement of anchors near the biceps should be avoided.
Anchors should be spaced out on the glenoid to prevent anchor encroachment. Anchors
should be placed approximately 1.5 mm onto the glenoid face.
Remplissage (Figure 11)
For off-track Hill-Sachs lesions
During labral repair, the timing of remplissage varies from surgeon to surgeon.
A burr is used to decorticate the Hill-Sachs lesion.
Next, a double-loaded suture anchor is inserted into the defect through a posterior portal
into the humeral head.
A penetrating grasper is then placed through the infraspinatus tendon and the posterior
capsule (1 cm inferior to where the portal entered the joint), retrieving one limb of the
suture.
This is repeated with an additional limb of the suture at a point distinct from the previous
suture passage.
The sutures are then tied in a fashion that draws the infraspinatus and capsule into the
lesion.
The knots are extraarticular and located in the subacromial space.

Figure 11 Arthroscopic images of a glenohumeral joint from the posterior portal show
remplissage. A, Image shows introduction of a narrow switching stick with appropriate trajectory

American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2016, pp 97-109.)

Preoperative Planning, Surgical Technique, Patient Positioning,
Technique/Procedures, Equipment
A meticulous preoperative plan is necessary to identify the appropriate procedure. The
quality and type of Bankart lesion, degree of glenoid bone loss, and nature of the Hill-
Sachs lesion must be assessed. A bony Bankart lesion with greater than 25% glenoid
bone loss requires an open Latarjet procedure (typically not performed in the immature
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:30 AM
AAOS | Shoulder Instability
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000034
21/28

population). This degree of bone loss precludes arthroscopic stabilization procedures. In
addition, an off-track Hill-Sachs lesion requires remplissage and standard arthroscopic
Bankart repair.
The surgeon should use the patient position (ie, beach-chair versus lateral decubitus)
that he or she is most comfortable with and should have various options available for
labral fixation. After diagnostic arthroscopy, the surgeon should prepare the glenoid and
labral tissue for fixation. The capsule and labrum is advanced using suture passing
devices and shifted onto the glenoid using anchors to reestablish the passive restraint to
anterior instability. Remplissage may be performed if indicated.
Postoperative Management
A shoulder immobilizer is applied while the patient is under anesthesia.
Patients are discharged home the same day and remain non–weight bearing on the affected
extremity for 6 weeks postoperatively.
For the first 3 weeks postoperatively, only elbow and wrist range of motion is allowed.
From 3 to 6 weeks postoperatively, passive range of motion of the shoulder with flexion is
limited to 90°, external rotation is limited to 45°, and extension is limited to 20°.
At 6 weeks postoperatively, use of the shoulder immobilizer is discontinued, and active-
assisted range of motion is allowed, with a goal of full range of motion by 12 weeks
postoperatively.
At 12 weeks postoperatively, muscle strengthening is allowed with concentration on deltoid,
rotator cuff, scapular stabilizer, biceps, and triceps strength.
Lower body endurance exercises and running/cycling are allowed at 12 weeks postoperatively.
At 5 months postoperatively, aggressive strengthening and plyometric work can begin. In
throwing athletes, a return to throwing program is initiated.
At 6 months postoperatively, patients can return to full activity as tolerated if full range of
motion and functional sport-specific strength have been regained.

Postoperative Management

Postoperative management is focused on soft-tissue healing, with a gradual return of
motion and strength. Return to activity is guided by functional testing and specific
activity level.
Complications
Recurrent instability because of lack of capsular shift, glenoid bone loss (>25%), lack of
remplissage with an off-track lesion, and inadequate number of anchors
Infection
Stiffness in external rotation
Chondral injury
Axillary nerve injury
Superficial radial nerve injury (from traction holder)
Chondrolysis (risk factors include young age, intraarticular pain pump, and thermal surgical
devices)
Outcomes
Arthroscopic shoulder stabilization allows adolescent athletes to return to sporting activity.
Kasik et al24 conducted a systemic review of 11 studies that included 461 athletes and
reported a return to play rate of 81.5%.
Saper et al25 examined a cohort of athletes who played collision and contact sports and also
reported a high return to play rate (78.1%).
Surgical failure rates in the pediatric/adolescent population are higher than in the adult
population (12.5% to 51%).24,26-29

Outcomes
Although surgical techniques have evolved, pediatric and adolescent patients have a
higher rate of recurrent instability after surgical treatment than adults. The etiology is
multifactorial but is generally attributed to postoperative participation in high-risk
sporting activities.
